name: Grand Summoner Govannon

related.relation: the binder who holds Midgard's dead back from his calling

facts.text: Grand Summoner Govannon is the level-80 final of Summoner's Hall for all three realms' raids; the Offline DAoC build gives him 200,000 health (300,000 originally).

At 80% he grows stronger and calls a summoned sacrifice and a summoned demon. The sacrifice walks to his feet and is consumed there; once it has been consumed and the demon is dead, the Shade of Aelfgar rises and joins the fight, stunning with Aelfgar's Shout.
At 50% he drops his elven shape, becomes a demon, heals to full health and hits harder still.
He casts Govannon's Shroud of Agony (an area damage over time) and a bleeding Demon's Scar, sends a random attacker to a fixed spot, and cannot be hurt when drawn past his tether.
Allakhazam lists him as a level-80 demon. A period player wrote that you first see an elf caster, then a taller shape, and at 60% his true demon form; 43 people took close to 30 minutes.
Bot chat says he starts as an elf and finishes as a demon, and tells a 'shield node' story that the script does not have (hearsay).
Gofannon (Govannon) is the smith son of Don in the Welsh tales (to verify the spelling and role in the Mabinogion).
Aelfgar is an Old English name; aelf means elf and gar spear (to verify).
The Shade of Aelfgar rises only when the summoned sacrifice has reached Govannon and the summoned demon is dead; both are cleared when the fight resets.
When Govannon morphs into his demon form at half health he is restored to full health.

story:
Grand Summoner Govannon holds the deepest room of the Summoner's Hall, the hall under all three old frontiers, in a chamber laid out in the pattern of Legion's court. His name is a smith's from the old tales of the west; what he makes is bargains, and his material is the dead. Each realm tells him differently: Camelot's scholars say he was a mage of the old Britons who took a smith's name; the druids of Tir na Nog say he wears the stolen shape of one of the sidhe; Jordheim's skalds say there is no one under the shape at all.

He came to the empty sidhe hall, the realms' meeting place under their borders, and filled it with summoners: Cunovinda, his first student, Lossren the gatherer, Roesia the keeper of pain. Together they call the dead of Albion, Midgard and Hibernia through the floors of the frontier dungeons, and the dead who answer join the Lords of the Undead. Midgard's miners heard the calling in Dodens Gruva, and Aros bound them rather than let them go.

Every calling has a price, and Govannon pays his debts. When he is pressed, a sacrifice walks across the floor to his feet while a demon stands beside him; if the price is paid and the demon falls, his old creditor the Shade of Aelfgar rises out of the floor to collect, with the war-cry that killed him. At half his strength he drops the elven shape he was paid in long ago, and the demon steps out of it whole, as if the first half of the fight had happened to someone else. His power is the pattern of his room; drawn out of it he is only a shape. Each realm claims the first kill of him, and none of them has stopped the calling for longer than a season. What he is making with the souls, nobody agrees.

chapters.title: A Smith's Name
chapters.text:
In the old tales of the west, the tales the bards of Camelot learned from the Britons before Arthur, there was a smith among the children of Don called Gofannon, who forged for the gods and was the greatest maker of his age. The Grand Summoner of the hall under the frontiers carries his name, Govannon, and every realm agrees that he took it on purpose. They agree on nothing else.

The scholars of Camelot say he was a man once, a mage of the old Britons who studied the summoning of spirits in the years before Camelot, when such studies were not yet forbidden. He took the smith's name because he believed a summoner should be a maker, not a beggar, and that the dead were only another material, like iron. They say he went under the hills to find a place where the dead of every people could be reached, and did not come back up.

The druids of Tir na Nog say he was never a man. They say the shape he wears, a tall caster in fine robes with the sidhe's long face, belonged to one of the Good Folk of the hollow hills, and that he took it as payment for a bargain the druids will not describe, and wears it into every fight as an insult to Hibernia. The smith's name, they say, is only a joke on the sidhe, who were the makers of the hall he stole.

The skalds of Jordheim say there is no one under the shape at all. The Grand Summoner, in their telling, is a thing out of the same dark as the demons of Darkness Falls, and the elf and the name are both masks. They point to Aros the Spiritmaster, who saw a robed figure smile at him from the hall's floor as one craftsman smiles at another, and they say a thing that smiles like that at a binder of souls is a binder of souls itself, and nothing else.

chapters.title: The Hall Under the Borders
chapters.text:
The hall was there before him. Every realm's old frontier dungeon digs down to it: Albion's Hall of the Corrupt, Midgard's Dodens Gruva and, the Hibernians say, Marfach Caverns. Each has a stair at the bottom, and each stair ends on the same floor. The druids say the sidhe built it in an age before the realms had names, as a meeting place under the borders where the peoples of the three lands could speak without crossing into each other's country, and that the sidhe magickers and protectors who serve there now are the descendants of its first keepers. A high lord of the sidhe, Ard Tiarna Kieren, still walks its halls.

The meeting place fell empty in the long years when the peoples above stopped speaking to each other and began to fight. The druids say the sidhe kept it anyway, out of duty, the way a steward keeps a hall whose lord has died. Then the summoner came down one of the stairs, and the stewards found that their hall had a new lord.

He changed its rooms. He had been to Darkness Falls, the hall's sidhe say, and had stood in the court of the arch-demon Legion, and admired it, because he admires anything that holds a great many souls. So he laid the deepest rooms of the Summoner's Hall out in the pattern of Legion's court, wing for wing, so that the room where Legion sits in Darkness Falls is, in the Summoner's Hall, the room where Govannon sits. The players who first explored it said it at once: the place looks like Darkness Falls. It was built to.

The pattern is the source of his strength. That is the rule of his room the raids learn first. Inside the pattern, in the place where Legion's throne would stand, his power flows into him from every wing of the hall. Drawn out of it, past the edge of his room, he is only a shape, and a shape cannot be wounded; he simply walks back to his place and is whole.

chapters.title: The Calling
chapters.text:
Govannon calls. That is what the Summoner's Hall is for now, and what its summoners do all day and all night: they call the dead, of every realm at once, in every realm's tongue. The calling goes up through the stairs into the frontier dungeons above, and through the floors of the mines and tombs and halls of the old frontiers, and the dead who hear it get up and walk down toward it. When they arrive, they belong to the hall. The scholars of Allakhazam's age noted that the hall's mobs were all of one faction, the Lords of the Undead, and that striking one turned the rest against you; the faction is the hall's answerers, the dead who came when they were called.

He trained three summoners to call with him. Cunovinda came first, a name that means white hound in a tongue older than Camelot, and she is still his best student, and puts her enemies somewhere else rather than trade blows. Lossren is his gatherer, who collects the dead the calling brings and keeps the ones that arrive in pieces, and leaves them in a crowd around him. Roesia, who has a Camelot name and curses Albion's raiders in their own tongue, is the keeper of pain, who makes sure that every bargain the hall strikes hurts the one who strikes it. Each holds a room of the hall, and each must be passed before the deepest room.

Midgard's dead heard the calling in Dodens Gruva, when Jarl Ormarr's miners broke into a cold seam above the hall and heard voices in three tongues. The miners died, and their dead began to walk down toward the voices, and the spiritmaster Aros bound them to the mine rather than let the hall have them, and read their names every morning so that they would hear him louder. The robed figure who smiled at Aros from the floor of the hall, the skalds believe, was Govannon, admiring a rival.

chapters.title: The Price That Walks
chapters.text:
Every calling has a price, and Govannon always pays it. A sidhe magicker of the hall, who had been one of his students and spoke to a Midgard scholar for reasons of her own, put it plainly: a maker who does not pay is only a thief, and Govannon has never been a thief. The price is a soul, and it walks to him on its own feet.

That is the origin of what happens when a raid has hurt him to four-fifths of his strength. He stops to strike a bargain in front of them. He calls up a summoned demon to stand beside him and fight, and his strength rises with the bargain; and from the edge of the room a summoned sacrifice begins to walk across the floor toward his feet, slowly, not looking at anyone. If it reaches him, it is consumed, and the price is paid. A raid that kills the sacrifice before it arrives denies the bargain its price.

Paid prices are collected. Govannon has one old creditor, from the first bargain he ever made, the one that bought him the hall or his shape or both, depending on who tells it. The creditor is the Shade of Aelfgar. Aelfgar is an Old English name, elf-spear, and Camelot's priests say he was a warrior of Albion in the age before Arthur who went under the hills to kill a summoner and died there, shouting his war-cry, and that his ghost was taken as part of the price of that first bargain and has served as its collector since. When a sacrifice has reached Govannon's feet and the demon of the bargain has fallen, Aelfgar rises out of the floor to collect what is owed, and the war-cry he died with comes out of him again, and everyone near him is struck motionless by it. He fights beside the summoner until he is put down. The druids say he is not Govannon's servant, only his creditor, and that this is worse.

chapters.title: The Shape He Was Paid In
chapters.text:
Raids that reach the deepest room see an elf caster first, tall and robed, with a long sidhe face. The first players who fought him recorded that he grew taller as he weakened, and that at a point in his strength he turned into his true form, a demon. The hall's sidhe say the elf is the shape he was paid in, long ago, and that he wears it until it is no longer worth wearing. At half his strength he drops it. The elf splits, and the demon steps out of it, and the demon is whole: every wound the raid gave the elf belongs to the elf, and the demon has none of them. He hits harder in that shape than in any other, as if the elf had been holding him back.

That is the second rule of his room, and the cruellest: a raid kills him twice, and the second time from the beginning.

Each realm reads the change its own way. The druids of Tir na Nog say the elf was a real sidhe whom he unmade to take the shape, and that every time a raid sees the demon step out of the elf they are watching a murder repeated. The scholars of Camelot say he was a man who became a demon by his own studies, and that he wears the elf to mock the sidhe whose hall he took. The skalds of Jordheim say the demon is all there ever was, and the elf a mask, and that the healing proves it: a mask takes the blows and is thrown away.

The magicker who had been his student said something none of the three realms say. She said he does not know either. She said that when the elf splits, there is a moment before the demon speaks when the face in the middle looks surprised, every time, as if he had forgotten again which one of them he was.

chapters.title: The Agony and the Scar
chapters.text:
His room has its own ways of hurting the living, and each came from something he made. The first is the Shroud of Agony, a cloak of pain he draws around himself and lets fall on whoever stands near him, eating at them slowly; the magicker said he wove it from the last breath of the first soul he ever bargained for, and that it remembers the dying and shares it. The second is the Demon's Scar, the wound his demon shape leaves, which bleeds and keeps bleeding; it is the mark of the bargain, she said, a debt opened in the flesh that does not close until it is paid.

The third is the gallery. When a fighter has annoyed him, Govannon sends him elsewhere, up out of the fight to a fixed place on a ledge of the room, high above the floor, where the bound of the hall stand and watch the fights below. The hall's sidhe call it the gallery of witnesses. The summoner wants his bargains watched, they say, because a bargain no one sees is only a theft, and so he sends a living witness up to stand among the dead ones for a while. The fighter climbs down. The dead do not.

His room is guarded at every door by its stewards, the sidhe protectors and magickers, black and grey nobles of the hall's old court, and deep wolves that came down the stairs from the frontiers and never went back. Their faction is the summoner's; to strike one is to make enemies of all. Each realm's raid fights its way through them, past the three summoners, to his door, and each realm's raid meets the other realms' raids on the way in, because the hall is the only place where all three realms come together, and they have never once come together in peace.

chapters.title: Three Claims
chapters.text:
Every realm says it killed the Grand Summoner first. The three accounts cannot all be true, and each realm tells its own as history.

Albion's chronicle says a company of the Hall of the Corrupt's own knights, who had cleared the hall above and gone down its stair to see where the dead were going, reached the deepest room under Sir Edric of Caer Ulfwych and slew the summoner in his demon shape, and that the Shade of Aelfgar, freed for a moment, knelt to Sir Edric before he faded. Camelot's priests still pray for Aelfgar on the day of that kill.

Midgard's account says the first kill was made by forty-three of Jordheim and Glenlock, who came down the stair of Dodens Gruva past the jarl's hound under Thorkel Hallsson, fought through the summoners for half a day, and killed the summoner in a little under the time it takes a skald to sing the long lay of the binding of the wolf. The skalds say that when he died, the picks in Dodens Gruva stopped for a moment, and Aros the Spiritmaster looked up from his reading.

Hibernia's account says the first kill was made by the Good Folk of the hall themselves, with Hibernia's help: that a company out of Marfach under the ranger Aoife ni Riain found the sidhe stewards willing to stand aside for once, because the stewards wanted their hall back, and that Ard Tiarna Kieren watched the summoner die and did not lift a hand to save him. The druids say that is the true reason the sidhe of the hall still serve him: they waited too long, and when he came back, they were afraid.

He came back after all three, in a season or less, because the pattern of the room holds his place for him, and the calling began again.

chapters.title: What He Is Making
chapters.text:
Govannon is a maker, and a maker makes something. The souls the hall calls are his material, and he has been working them since before Camelot. Nobody knows what the work is, and the realms disagree as usual.

The scholars of Camelot say he is making an army: the Lords of the Undead, the dead of every realm in one host, bound to the hall and waiting for the day when the realms above have exhausted each other in their war and there is no one left to stop the dead walking up the three stairs at once. The druids of Tir na Nog say he is making a hall, a second Darkness Falls under the borders, a court of his own to rival Legion's, and that the sidhe were only the first of the stewards he will need. The skalds of Jordheim say he is making nothing at all, that a thing out of the dark only takes, and that the smith's name is the last and best of his jokes.

The magicker who had been his student gave a fourth answer, and the Midgard scholar who heard it wrote it down and then would not discuss it. She said he is making a bridge. She said that under the hall there is a place where the dead of all three realms are the same, and that he is building a way across to it out of the souls of the three realms, one bargain at a time, and that when it is finished he will go across, and the bridge will come with him, and the realms above will find that their dead have nowhere else to go.

Each realm's raids go down to the deepest room to stop the work for a season. Midgard's go for one more reason. In Dodens Gruva, at the head of the stair, Aros the Spiritmaster reads the names of his miners every morning, and has promised that when the calling stops, they may go. Every raid that kills Govannon gives them a season of quiet. None of them has given them more.

legend: Govannon is two fights. At 80% kill the sacrifice before it reaches his feet, or the Shade of Aelfgar comes once the demon dies; stun break for the shade's shout. At 50% he turns demon and heals to full, so pace your power: the second half is the real fight. Don't drag him off his spot, he can't be hurt past his tether. Period raids took about 40 people and half an hour. The shield node story is old raid talk; nobody has found the node. Bring the whole realm: period accounts put the hall at four to five groups and the summoner at about forty people and half an hour. Clear all three summoners first, then rest. Healers, expect the Shroud of Agony on the melee for the whole fight and the Demon's Scar on whoever holds him.

loremasterTopic.text: The Grand Summoner, named for a smith of the old tales because he too is a maker; what he makes is bargains. He wears a sidhe's shape until half his strength is gone, and then the demon steps out of it, whole. Stop his sacrifice reaching his feet, or the Shade of Aelfgar comes to collect.

bookPage: Of the bargains of the Grand Summoner, from a sidhe magicker who had been his student, as near as I could follow her. Every calling has a price, she said, and he always pays it, because a maker who does not pay is only a thief. The price walks to him on its own feet. If it arrives, the debt is settled, and the one he owes, an old ghost named Aelfgar, comes up out of the floor to take what is owed. If it does not arrive, he must find another way to pay, and he does not like that. She said the elf you see is the shape he was paid in, long ago. She would not say what paid it.
